name: Circuit Breaker
oneLineDefinition: A circuit breaker watches the calls to a dependency and, once too many fail, stops sending calls and fails them instantly for a while, so a down dependency can't tie up the whole system.
definition:
A circuit breaker wraps the calls your service makes to something it depends on - a database, a payment provider, another service - and monitors those calls. It has three states:

- closed - the normal, healthy state; calls flow straight through (similar to a closed electrical circuit)
- open - state reached after too many recent failures; calls fail instantly, without even trying the dependency
- half-open - state reached after a short cooling-off wait period; one test call is let through to see if the dependency is back

It starts in closed state and switches to open state when failures pile up. After a short cooling-off wait period, it switches to half-open state. From that state, a successful test call closes it again; a failed one opens it back up for another wait.

{{figure:the-three-states}}

Why not just rely on a timeout? Because a timeout is not free. It caps how long one call waits, but while the dependency is down, every new call still waits out the full timeout before giving up - tying up threads, connections, and queue slots at the worst possible moment. An outage usually stays down for a while, rather than clearing on its own within seconds. So instead of every call waiting out the full timeout for the whole outage, the breaker makes them fail right away. Pulling traffic away also gives the struggling dependency room to recover. Failing instantly makes room for a planned fallback - a cached value, a simpler path, a clear error message - but that fallback is work your application has to do; the breaker only creates the opening.

The main design decision is what exactly each breaker protects. Make its scope too broad and one small part failing trips the breaker for calls that would have worked fine. Make it too narrow and you end up with a breaker for everything, each one slower to notice trouble and each needing its own tuning. Nearly every ecosystem ships a circuit-breaker library, so writing the code is rarely the hard part. The common problem is a breaker added in a hurry: its trip thresholds get set once and never looked at again, and no one has decided what should actually happen when it trips.
whenItApplies: The dependency tends to fail in bursts. When it breaks, many calls fail together in a short window rather than one unlucky call here and there.
Waiting for the timeout costs more than failing fast. Every call stuck waiting holds a thread, a connection, or a queue slot that the system needs back.
You have a fallback, or a fast error beats a slow one. A cached value, a simpler path, or a clear error returned instantly is better than making the caller wait.
The dependency recovers faster when you leave it alone. Pulling traffic off a struggling service can be what lets it catch up and come back.
tradeoffs: The breaker only makes the opening. The fallback is still the application's job: deciding what to do with that instant failure - a cached value, a degraded path, a clear error - is work you have to design.
Bad thresholds or scope can do real damage. Set them wrong and a breaker can trip healthy traffic, or waste a lot of resources at scale before anyone notices.
How narrowly to scope each breaker is a standing design problem. Scope it broadly and one part failing trips calls that were fine; scope it finely and there is far more breaker state to tune.
Fast failures skew your latency graphs. A flood of instant failures looks fast, so success and failure have to be graphed separately or the dashboards lie.

artifact.teaser: Send calls through an outage with timeouts only, then with a breaker - watch the wasted waiting time collapse.

figures.caption: The breaker starts closed, letting calls through. Too many failures trip it open, so calls fail instantly. After a cooldown it goes half-open and sends one test call: success closes it again, a failure opens it back up.

mechanism.caption: THE PATTERN, GENERAL
mechanism.blurb: The pattern at its core: a stream of calls to a dependency that goes down for a while, and a breaker that steps in so those calls fail instantly instead of each waiting out the full timeout.
mechanism.idea: While a dependency is down, a call with only a timeout still waits the full timeout before failing - and every waiting call holds a thread the system needs. A breaker notices the run of failures, trips open, and fails the next calls instantly instead of waiting. That frees the system and takes load off the dependency so it can recover.
mechanism.whatToTry: Send a burst of calls through an outage with timeouts only, then with a breaker. With only timeouts, every call waits the full time; the breaker trips after a few failures and the rest fail instantly, so far less time is wasted waiting.
